OBJECTS OF THE UNION

The objectives for which the Kaduna Valley Cooperative Union is established are:

1. To promote the economic interests of its members in accordance with cooperative principles, including the pooling of resources for the purchase of farm inputs, seedlings, fertilizers, and improved implements at favourable terms.

2. To facilitate the marketing and sale of members' agricultural produce, including maize, sorghum, groundnuts, and irrigated vegetables, through collective bargaining and coordinated distribution channels.

3. To provide credit facilities for members, either directly or through approved financial institutions, for the purpose of expanding agricultural production, livestock rearing, and related enterprises.

4. To acquire, hold, lease, or otherwise deal with land, buildings, warehouses, stores, vehicles, and other property necessary or convenient for the achievement of the Union's objects.

5. To organize training programs, demonstrations, and extension services for members on modern farming techniques, soil conservation, water management, and post-harvest handling.

6. To establish and maintain processing facilities, including mills, shellers, dryers, and storage structures, for the benefit of members and the wider farming community.

7. To act as a channel for the distribution of government subsidies, relief materials, and development assistance intended for agricultural purposes.

8. To engage in any other lawful activity that may be conducive to or necessary for the attainment of the foregoing objects, provided that the Union shall not undertake activities for the primary purpose of profit-making for distribution to members.

---

MEMBERSHIP

Membership of the Union shall be open to:

(a) Any individual engaged in farming, livestock rearing, or agro-processing within the geographical area of operation of the Union, being not less than eighteen years of age.

(b) Any registered cooperative society whose membership is principally engaged in agricultural production and which seeks affiliation with the Union for the purpose of collective advancement.

(c) Any person admitted by the Committee of the Union in accordance with the Bye-Laws, provided such person subscribes to the objects of the Union and undertakes to abide by its rules.

Every applicant for membership shall complete an application form prescribed by the Committee, and admission shall be by resolution of the Committee at a meeting convened for that purpose. No person shall be admitted to membership without payment of the prescribed entrance fee and the minimum share subscription as determined from time to time by the general meeting.

Membership shall cease upon death, resignation, expulsion in accordance with the Bye-Laws, or upon the winding up of the Union. A member who has been expelled shall have the right of appeal to the annual general meeting.

---

RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS OF MEMBERS

Every member shall have the right to:

(i) Participate in the general meetings of the Union and vote on all matters brought before such meetings, in accordance with the principle of one member, one vote.

(ii) Be eligible for election to the Committee or any other office of the Union, subject to the qualifications and disqualifications prescribed in the Bye-Laws.

Conversion note: 4,450 tonnes seed cotton × 0.38 = 1,691 tonnes ginned. The reported 1,500 tonnes
reflects a 11.3% deduction for moisture and foreign matter at the gin, which is within the normal
range for the season. The cooperative has been asked to keep the gin tickets on file for the Union
audit in January.

Weather and crop conditions:

- Rainfall was generally adequate through July, but a dry spell in the second half of August
  affected boll development on the Dutsin-Ma and Bakori clusters. FCPC reported that the dry spell
  was less severe than the one that affected Kudan Multipurpose Farmers (see maize section), but it
  still reduced yields on non-irrigated plots by an estimated 8–10%.
- Irrigation: The Funtua town cluster has access to two boreholes and a small dam. Irrigation was
  applied on about 60% of the cluster's area during the dry spell. The remaining 40% (furthest from
  the water source) suffered the most.
- Pests: Bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) was the main problem, especially in Maska and Bakori.
  FCPC applied three rounds of insecticide (cypermethrin) between August and October. The
  cooperative also reported some aphid infestation in September, but it was controlled. No
  significant damage from jassids was reported this year.
- Weeding: Labour shortage was an issue in late July, similar to other cooperatives in the zone.
  Some fields in Bakori had a noticeable weed load, which likely contributed to the lower yield
  there.

Quality notes:

In the harvest report, the cotton_tonnes_harvested_2024 for Funtua Cotton Producers Cooperative is 1500 tonnes. Record status: current.

- Staple length and strength were assessed as average to good. The buying agent (Northern Cotton
  Ginners) has accepted the bulk of the crop at Grade II. A small lot from Dutsin-Ma (about 40
  tonnes seed cotton) was downgraded to Grade III due to staining from rain during the first
  picking.
- The cooperative plans to switch to a more pest-tolerant variety next season. They have requested
  seed from the Institute for Agricultural Research (IAR) Samaru for a trial plot in 2025.

Comparison to previous season (for reference only, not part of the current record):

- 2023 cotton production for FCPC was approximately 1,280 tonnes ginned, on 1,150 hectares (yield
  1.11 t/ha). The 2024 figure is therefore an increase of about 17% in production and 8% in yield.
  The improvement is attributed to better pest control and the expansion of irrigated area.
- Note: The 2023 figure is an estimate provided by the cooperative secretary; the Union did not
  have a field officer visit that season due to staffing constraints. Use with caution if comparing
  trends.

Recommendations:

1. The Union should consider FCPC's request for a second borehole at the Maska cluster. The
   cooperative estimates that this would add 150–200 ha of irrigated cotton and reduce yield
   variability.
2. The cooperative should be encouraged to submit their gin tickets and weighbridge records
   promptly for the January audit. The current figure is final, but the supporting documents are
   still required for the Union's records.
3. Pest control: FCPC is considering a shift to integrated pest management (IPM) for 2025. The
   Union's extension officer should follow up on this and provide training if needed.

Mixed crops entry. The harvest report states the mixed_crops_tonnes_harvested_2024 for Kafanchan Mixed Farmers Cooperative as 2100 tonnes. Record status: current. This figure is current and represents the total tonnage from the cooperative's mixed-crop fields, which are planted in a relay/intercrop system rather than as a single commodity. The area figure of 1,750 ha is the combined field size for these plots; the yield of 1.20 t/ha is an average across the mixture and should not be interpreted as the yield of any one crop. The mixture consists primarily of maize and soybean planted together, with some groundnut and sorghum interplanted on the lighter soils. The cooperative has used this system for the past four seasons, and the 2024 result is broadly in line with their five-year average, though slightly below the exceptional 2023 season when mixed fields produced approximately 2,250 tonnes (that figure is from the cooperative's own records and was not field-verified; it is included here only as a point of reference and is not part of the current record).

Field notes and verification remarks. The cooperative's weighbridge is calibrated annually by the Ministry of Weights and Measures; the 2024 calibration certificate was sighted during the visit. A. Yusuf cross-checked the tonnage for maize and soybean against the delivery receipts from the Kafanchan market and the feed mill at Kwoi; the receipts matched the cooperative's figures within 2% for both crops. For mixed crops, the verification was less straightforward because the produce is not sold as a single lot. The cooperative sells maize and soybean from the mixed fields separately after threshing, and the 2,100-tonne figure is the sum of those components plus the small amounts of groundnut and sorghum that were harvested from the same plots. The cooperative's secretary stated that the breakdown is approximately 1,100 tonnes of maize, 800 tonnes of soybean, and 200 tonnes of combined groundnut/sorghum from the mixed fields. These component figures are estimates made at the time of the visit and have not been independently verified; the total of 2,100 tonnes is the figure that should be used for Union records.

Storage and quality. The cooperative stores most of the mixed-crop output in a central warehouse at Kafanchan (capacity 2,500 tonnes). At the time of the visit, the warehouse was holding approximately 1,400 tonnes of maize and soybean from the mixed fields, with the remainder already sold. Moisture content of the stored grain was measured at 11.5% for maize and 10.8% for soybean, both within acceptable limits. The cooperative reported no significant quality complaints from buyers this season. One minor issue: the storage ledger did not separately record the tonnage of groundnut and sorghum from the mixed fields; these were lumped together as "other". This is a bookkeeping matter and does not affect the total figure, but the cooperative has been advised to keep separate entries in future so that the component breakdown can be verified.
2024 Harvest Report – Member Cooperatives
Zaria District Maize Growers Association (ZDMGA) – Supplementary Yield Analysis

Addendum to the main harvest report for the 2024 season. This section covers the yield per hectare analysis for ZDMGA, with comparisons to the regional averages for the Northern Guinea Savannah zone. The figures below supplement the tonnage and verification remarks recorded in the main body of the report.

1. Yield Calculation Basis

The yield per hectare figures in this addendum are calculated using the planted area as declared by the cooperative at the beginning of the season, not the harvested area. The cooperative reported a total planted area of 1,250 hectares for maize in 2024. This area was confirmed through the field inspection carried out during the mid-season visit; GPS measurements were taken for a sample of 60 fields, and the extrapolated total was within 3% of the cooperative's declared figure.

For the yield calculation, the cooperative's total maize production for the season is taken from the verified tonnage figures in the main report. The maize output from the mixed fields is included in this total, as the cooperative sells maize from those fields separately after threshing.

2. ZDMGA Maize Yield – 2024

According to the harvest report, the yield_per_hectare_2024 for Zaria District Maize Growers Association is 2.8 tonnes/ha. Record status: current. This figure is current and is the one to be used for Union records. It is based on the verified total maize production of 3,500 tonnes divided by the confirmed planted area of 1,250 hectares. The calculation is straightforward: 3,500 ÷ 1,250 = 2.8. There is no rounding involved; the division works out exactly.

3. Regional Comparison

The table below compares the ZDMGA maize yield to the regional averages for the 2024 season, as compiled by the Union's statistics unit from the reports of the member cooperatives in the zone.

| Cooperative / Zone | Maize Yield (tonnes/ha) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ZDMGA (Zaria) | 2.8 | Current figure, verified this season |
| Northern Guinea Savannah zone average | 2.3 | All member cooperatives |
| Kaduna South cluster average | 2.1 | Excluding ZDMGA |
| Best performing cooperative (Kudan) | 3.1 | Smallholder, 480 ha planted |

The ZDMGA yield is 0.5 tonnes/ha above the zone average, which places the cooperative in the upper quartile of the 14 member cooperatives reporting maize yields this season. The Kudan cooperative's 3.1 tonnes/ha is the highest in the zone; the ZDMGA figure is second highest.

4. Agronomic Commentary

The yield analysis indicates that the ZDMGA performance is broadly in line with expectations for the zone given the rainfall pattern. The 2024 season had a slightly above-average total rainfall in the Zaria area, but the distribution was uneven, with a dry spell of about 12 days in late July. The cooperative's early planting (most fields were sown by May 20) meant that the crop was at the tasseling stage during the dry spell, which can reduce yield potential. Despite this, the yield held up well, which the extension agent attributes to the drought-tolerant varieties and the fact that the cooperative was able to carry out supplementary irrigation on about 150 hectares of the most affected fields using the small dam at the Kafanchan site.

One point of note: the yield figure of 2.8 tonnes/ha is for the whole maize area, including the mixed fields. If the maize component of the mixed fields is excluded, the yield on the pure maize fields alone would be approximately 2.9 tonnes/ha. The cooperative's secretary indicated that the pure maize fields (about 950 hectares) produced approximately 2,750 tonnes, which gives a yield of about 2.9 tonnes/ha. However, the 2.8 tonnes/ha figure is the one that should be used for Union records, as it is based on the verified total production and the total planted area.

6. Comparison with Previous Year

Total production for the 2024 season is 18,182 tonnes across the crops listed above. This compares with 16,940 tonnes reported for the 2023 season, an increase of 1,242 tonnes, or approximately 7.3 per cent. The increase is attributed mainly to the expansion of maize area in the Kaduna South cluster (up by 210 ha) and improved sorghum yields in Birnin Gwari, where the early rains were more favourable than in 2023.

The 2023 figure of 16,940 tonnes was revised in March 2024 when two cooperatives (Giwa and Soba) submitted corrected area figures. The corrected 2023 total is the one shown here; the original return had been 17,120 tonnes. The difference arose from a double-counting of fallow land in the Giwa return.

Per-hectare yields are broadly stable. The zone average maize yield rose from 2.2 tonnes/ha in 2023 to 2.3 tonnes/ha in 2024, while sorghum remained at 1.8 tonnes/ha and millet at 1.5 tonnes/ha. The ZDMGA maize yield of 2.8 tonnes/ha is unchanged from the 2023 verified figure; the cooperative's management attributes this to the same field rotation pattern being maintained.

7. Market Conditions and Sales Outlook

Prices at the time of writing (early December) are as follows, based on the Zaria central market and the Kaduna grain exchange:

- Maize: ₦285,000 – ₦310,000 per tonne, depending on grade and moisture content. The lower end is for grain with moisture above 13 per cent; most cooperatives are drying to 12 per cent before sale.
- Sorghum: ₦240,000 – ₦260,000 per tonne.
- Millet: ₦265,000 – ₦280,000 per tonne.

These prices are roughly 12–15 per cent above the same period last year. The increase is driven by strong demand from poultry feed mills in Kaduna and by reduced supplies from the southern part of the country, where flooding affected the early harvest. Several cooperatives have already signed forward contracts for delivery in January; the ZDMGA has contracted 800 tonnes of maize at ₦300,000 per tonne, which the secretary regards as a satisfactory price given the moisture content clause in the contract.
8. Field Notes and Challenges

The following notes were compiled from the December zonal meetings and from the extension officers' end-of-season returns. They are included for the record and for planning purposes; they have not been audited to the same standard as the production tables in Section 3.

- Weather: The early rains (May–June) were generally good across the zone, but there was a dry spell of about 11 days in the third week of July that affected flowering in some early-planted maize fields. The Kaduna South cluster reports that this dry spell reduced potential yields on roughly 15% of their maize area, though the overall cluster figure still improved because of the area expansion. In Birnin Gwari, the rains were steadier and the sorghum crop benefited; several farmers described the season as "the best we have had since 2021."
- The dry spell also delayed the second weeding in some millet plots. Extension staff note that fields where the second weeding was delayed by more than a week showed noticeably more striga infestation by late August. This is consistent with the observations from 2022, though the affected area is smaller this year.
- Pests: Fall armyworm pressure was moderate, lower than in 2023. The early spraying programme organised by the cooperative union in July appears to have been effective. The ZDMGA reports that only 3 of their 42 maize fields required a second spray, compared with 11 in 2023. The cost of the programme was shared between the cooperatives and the zonal office; the total expenditure was ₦1.85 million, which is within the budgeted amount.
- Quelea birds caused localised damage to sorghum in the Birnin Gwari and Igabi areas. The damage was confined to fields near the riverine strips. One farmer in Birnin Gwari, Alhaji Musa, said, "We lost maybe two bags from the edge of the field, but the birds came early and the crop was still soft, so it could have been worse." No cooperative has reported losses exceeding 2% of its harvested tonnage.
- Farmer feedback: There is broad satisfaction with the improved sorghum varieties distributed in 2023. Several cooperatives have asked for a larger allocation of the ICSV 400 seed for the 2025 season. However, there were complaints about the late delivery of the maize seed in the Giwa cluster; the seed arrived in the second week of June, after some farmers had already planted other varieties. The zonal office is aware of this and has noted it in the procurement review.
- Storage: The new drying floors at the Kaduna South central store are being used more than expected. The cooperative secretary there reports that the floors are handling about 60% of the cluster's maize before bagging, up from 40% in 2023. The remaining maize is still being dried on tarpaulins. Moisture readings taken at delivery show that the tarpaulin-dried grain averages 13.5% moisture, slightly above the 12% target, while the floor-dried grain averages 11.8%.
- Labour: Harvest labour was generally available, though wages rose by about 8% compared with 2023. The daily rate in the southern part of the zone is now ₦3,500 for a full day, and some cooperatives report that they had to pay up to ₦4,000 to secure workers during the peak of the maize harvest. This has increased the cost per tonne of harvesting by roughly ₦600–₦800, which is reflected in the cost analysis in Section 9.
- One issue was raised by the Giwa cooperative regarding the corrected 2023 area figures. The secretary there has confirmed that the double-counting of fallow land has been resolved and that the corrected figure of 16,940 tonnes is the one they will use in their own records going forward. He noted that the original return had been based on a hand-drawn map that included a plot that was not cultivated in 2023.

The Union is registered with the following objects:

CERTIFICATE OF REGISTRATION – KADUNA VALLEY COOPERATIVE UNION

Registration No: KDS/COOP/1998/0147

Date of Incorporation: 15th March, 1998

---

OBJECTS OF THE UNION

The objectives for which the Kaduna Valley Cooperative Union is established are:

1. To promote the economic interests of its members in accordance with cooperative principles, including the pooling of resources for the purchase of farm inputs, seedlings, fertilizers, and improved implements at favourable terms.

2. To facilitate the marketing and sale of members' agricultural produce, including maize, sorghum, groundnuts, and irrigated vegetables, through collective bargaining and coordinated distribution channels.

3. To provide credit facilities for members, either directly or through approved financial institutions, for the purpose of expanding agricultural production, livestock rearing, and related enterprises.

4. To acquire, hold, lease, or otherwise deal with land, buildings, warehouses, stores, vehicles, and other property necessary or convenient for the achievement of the Union's objects.

5. To organize training programs, demonstrations, and extension services for members on modern farming techniques, soil conservation, water management, and post-harvest handling.

6. To establish and maintain processing facilities, including mills, shellers, dryers, and storage structures, for the benefit of members and the wider farming community.

7. To act as a channel for the distribution of government subsidies, relief materials, and development assistance intended for agricultural purposes.

8. To engage in any other lawful activity that may be conducive to or necessary for the attainment of the foregoing objects, provided that the Union shall not undertake activities for the primary purpose of profit-making for distribution to members.

---

MEMBERSHIP

Membership of the Union shall be open to:

(a) Any individual engaged in farming, livestock rearing, or agro-processing within the geographical area of operation of the Union, being not less than eighteen years of age.

(b) Any registered cooperative society whose membership is principally engaged in agricultural production and which seeks affiliation with the Union for the purpose of collective advancement.

(c) Any person admitted by the Committee of the Union in accordance with the Bye-Laws, provided such person subscribes to the objects of the Union and undertakes to abide by its rules.

Every applicant for membership shall complete an application form prescribed by the Committee, and admission shall be by resolution of the Committee at a meeting convened for that purpose. No person shall be admitted to membership without payment of the prescribed entrance fee and the minimum share subscription as determined from time to time by the general meeting.

Membership shall cease upon death, resignation, expulsion in accordance with the Bye-Laws, or upon the winding up of the Union. A member who has been expelled shall have the right of appeal to the annual general meeting.

---

RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS OF MEMBERS

Every member shall have the right to:

(i) Participate in the general meetings of the Union and vote on all matters brought before such meetings, in accordance with the principle of one member, one vote.

(ii) Be eligible for election to the Committee or any other office of the Union, subject to the qualifications and disqualifications prescribed in the Bye-Laws.

This figure is current and represents the total tonnage from the cooperative's mixed-crop fields, which are planted in a relay/intercrop system rather than as a single commodity. The area figure of 1,750 ha is the combined field size for these plots; the yield of 1.20 t/ha is an average across the mixture and should not be interpreted as the yield of any one crop. The mixture consists primarily of maize and soybean planted together, with some groundnut and sorghum interplanted on the lighter soils. The cooperative has used this system for the past four seasons, and the 2024 result is broadly in line with their five-year average, though slightly below the exceptional 2023 season when mixed fields produced approximately 2,250 tonnes (that figure is from the cooperative's own records and was not field-verified; it is included here only as a point of reference and is not part of the current record).

2024 Harvest Report – Member Cooperatives
Zaria District Maize Growers Association (ZDMGA) – Supplementary Yield Analysis

Addendum to the main harvest report for the 2024 season. This section covers the yield per hectare analysis for ZDMGA, with comparisons to the regional averages for the Northern Guinea Savannah zone. The figures below supplement the tonnage and verification remarks recorded in the main body of the report.

1. Yield Calculation Basis

The yield per hectare figures in this addendum are calculated using the planted area as declared by the cooperative at the beginning of the season, not the harvested area. The cooperative reported a total planted area of 1,250 hectares for maize in 2024. This area was confirmed through the field inspection carried out during the mid-season visit; GPS measurements were taken for a sample of 60 fields, and the extrapolated total was within 3% of the cooperative's declared figure.

For the yield calculation, the cooperative's total maize production for the season is taken from the verified tonnage figures in the main report. The maize output from the mixed fields is included in this total, as the cooperative sells maize from those fields separately after threshing.

2. ZDMGA Maize Yield – 2024

According to the harvest report, the yield_per_hectare_2024 for Zaria District Maize Growers Association is 2.8 tonnes/ha. Record status: current. This figure is current and is the one to be used for Union records. It is based on the verified total maize production of 3,500 tonnes divided by the confirmed planted area of 1,250 hectares. The calculation is straightforward: 3,500 ÷ 1,250 = 2.8. There is no rounding involved; the division works out exactly.

3. Regional Comparison

The table below compares the ZDMGA maize yield to the regional averages for the 2024 season, as compiled by the Union's statistics unit from the reports of the member cooperatives in the zone.

| Cooperative / Zone | Maize Yield (tonnes/ha) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ZDMGA (Zaria) | 2.8 | Current figure, verified this season |
| Northern Guinea Savannah zone average | 2.3 | All member cooperatives |
| Kaduna South cluster average | 2.1 | Excluding ZDMGA |
| Best performing cooperative (Kudan) | 3.1 | Smallholder, 480 ha planted |

The ZDMGA yield is 0.5 tonnes/ha above the zone average, which places the cooperative in the upper quartile of the 14 member cooperatives reporting maize yields this season. The Kudan cooperative's 3.1 tonnes/ha is the highest in the zone; the ZDMGA figure is second highest.

4. Agronomic Commentary

The yield analysis indicates that the ZDMGA performance is broadly in line with expectations for the zone given the rainfall pattern. The 2024 season had a slightly above-average total rainfall in the Zaria area, but the distribution was uneven, with a dry spell of about 12 days in late July. The cooperative's early planting (most fields were sown by May 20) meant that the crop was at the tasseling stage during the dry spell, which can reduce yield potential. Despite this, the yield held up well, which the extension agent attributes to the drought-tolerant varieties and the fact that the cooperative was able to carry out supplementary irrigation on about 150 hectares of the most affected fields using the small dam at the Kafanchan site.

One point of note: the yield figure of 2.8 tonnes/ha is for the whole maize area, including the mixed fields. If the maize component of the mixed fields is excluded, the yield on the pure maize fields alone would be approximately 2.9 tonnes/ha. The cooperative's secretary indicated that the pure maize fields (about 950 hectares) produced approximately 2,750 tonnes, which gives a yield of about 2.9 tonnes/ha. However, the 2.8 tonnes/ha figure is the one that should be used for Union records, as it is based on the verified total production and the total planted area.

6. Comparison with Previous Year

Total production for the 2024 season is 18,182 tonnes across the crops listed above. This compares with 16,940 tonnes reported for the 2023 season, an increase of 1,242 tonnes, or approximately 7.3 per cent. The increase is attributed mainly to the expansion of maize area in the Kaduna South cluster (up by 210 ha) and improved sorghum yields in Birnin Gwari, where the early rains were more favourable than in 2023.

The 2023 figure of 16,940 tonnes was revised in March 2024 when two cooperatives (Giwa and Soba) submitted corrected area figures. The corrected 2023 total is the one shown here; the original return had been 17,120 tonnes. The difference arose from a double-counting of fallow land in the Giwa return.

Per-hectare yields are broadly stable. The zone average maize yield rose from 2.2 tonnes/ha in 2023 to 2.3 tonnes/ha in 2024, while sorghum remained at 1.8 tonnes/ha and millet at 1.5 tonnes/ha. The ZDMGA maize yield of 2.8 tonnes/ha is unchanged from the 2023 verified figure; the cooperative's management attributes this to the same field rotation pattern being maintained.

7. Market Conditions and Sales Outlook

Prices at the time of writing (early December) are as follows, based on the Zaria central market and the Kaduna grain exchange:

- Maize: ₦285,000 – ₦310,000 per tonne, depending on grade and moisture content. The lower end is for grain with moisture above 13 per cent; most cooperatives are drying to 12 per cent before sale.
- Sorghum: ₦240,000 – ₦260,000 per tonne.
- Millet: ₦265,000 – ₦280,000 per tonne.

These prices are roughly 12–15 per cent above the same period last year. The increase is driven by strong demand from poultry feed mills in Kaduna and by reduced supplies from the southern part of the country, where flooding affected the early harvest. Several cooperatives have already signed forward contracts for delivery in January; the ZDMGA has contracted 800 tonnes of maize at ₦300,000 per tonne, which the secretary regards as a satisfactory price given the moisture content clause in the contract.

8. Field Notes and Challenges

The following notes were compiled from the December zonal meetings and from the extension officers' end-of-season returns. They are included for the record and for planning purposes; they have not been audited to the same standard as the production tables in Section 3.

- Weather: The early rains (May–June) were generally good across the zone, but there was a dry spell of about 11 days in the third week of July that affected flowering in some early-planted maize fields. The Kaduna South cluster reports that this dry spell reduced potential yields on roughly 15% of their maize area, though the overall cluster figure still improved because of the area expansion. In Birnin Gwari, the rains were steadier and the sorghum crop benefited; several farmers described the season as "the best we have had since 2021."
- The dry spell also delayed the second weeding in some millet plots. Extension staff note that fields where the second weeding was delayed by more than a week showed noticeably more striga infestation by late August. This is consistent with the observations from 2022, though the affected area is smaller this year.
- Pests: Fall armyworm pressure was moderate, lower than in 2023. The early spraying programme organised by the cooperative union in July appears to have been effective. The ZDMGA reports that only 3 of their 42 maize fields required a second spray, compared with 11 in 2023. The cost of the programme was shared between the cooperatives and the zonal office; the total expenditure was ₦1.85 million, which is within the budgeted amount.
- Quelea birds caused localised damage to sorghum in the Birnin Gwari and Igabi areas. The damage was confined to fields near the riverine strips. One farmer in Birnin Gwari, Alhaji Musa, said, "We lost maybe two bags from the edge of the field, but the birds came early and the crop was still soft, so it could have been worse." No cooperative has reported losses exceeding 2% of its harvested tonnage.
- Farmer feedback: There is broad satisfaction with the improved sorghum varieties distributed in 2023. Several cooperatives have asked for a larger allocation of the ICSV 400 seed for the 2025 season. However, there were complaints about the late delivery of the maize seed in the Giwa cluster; the seed arrived in the second week of June, after some farmers had already planted other varieties. The zonal office is aware of this and has noted it in the procurement review.
- Storage: The new drying floors at the Kaduna South central store are being used more than expected. The cooperative secretary there reports that the floors are handling about 60% of the cluster's maize before bagging, up from 40% in 2023. The remaining maize is still being dried on tarpaulins. Moisture readings taken at delivery show that the tarpaulin-dried grain averages 13.5% moisture, slightly above the 12% target, while the floor-dried grain averages 11.8%.
- Labour: Harvest labour was generally available, though wages rose by about 8% compared with 2023. The daily rate in the southern part of the zone is now ₦3,500 for a full day, and some cooperatives report that they had to pay up to ₦4,000 to secure workers during the peak of the maize harvest. This has increased the cost per tonne of harvesting by roughly ₦600–₦800, which is reflected in the cost analysis in Section 9.
- One issue was raised by the Giwa cooperative regarding the corrected 2023 area figures. The secretary there has confirmed that the double-counting of fallow land has been resolved and that the corrected figure of 16,940 tonnes is the one they will use in their own records going forward. He noted that the original return had been based on a hand-drawn map that included a plot that was not cultivated in 2023.
